title: PISA 2025 Will Reveal a Technology Sweet Spot
author: The Digital Delusion
summary: In advance of the September 2025 PISA data release, this analysis predicts that international test results will appear to show a technology 'sweet spot' where light classroom technology use outperforms both no use and heavy use, and argues in advance why that apparent finding will be a statistical artifact rather than genuine evidence. The author traces the pattern back to PISA 2012, where only the most technologically saturated systems (Australia, Denmark, Sweden) showed an inverted-U relationship, and demonstrates across the 2012, 2015, 2018, and 2022 cycles that the apparent advantage of light technology use grows precisely as the 'zero-use' comparison group shrinks and becomes composed of atypical students. Using a glasses-wearing analogy, the piece explains that once nearly everyone in a population uses a technology, the shrinking non-user group can no longer serve as a meaningful baseline for what an average student would experience without it. The author rules out competing explanations, showing that countries whose technology saturation increased fastest were no more likely to see overall achievement gains, and that the pattern held even when accounting for the parallel shift to computer-based testing. The piece is explicitly a falsifiable prediction: if the pattern strengthens as forecast, it supports the comparison-group explanation; if the zero-use group rebounds and the advantage persists anyway, the explanation is wrong.
points: Predicts, before the data is released, that PISA 2025 will show a technology 'sweet spot' (an inverted-U between tech use and achievement) and stakes the entire piece on that being falsifiable rather than retrofitted after the fact.

Shows the apparent advantage of light technology use statistically strengthens as a country's zero-use student group shrinks and becomes less representative (r values from -.41 in 2012 to -.68 in 2015 to -.57 in 2018), across socioeconomic and school-fixed-effects controls.

Rules out the alternative explanation that increasingly tech-saturated countries are simply getting better at using technology, finding no correlation between saturation growth and overall achievement gains across any PISA cycle examined.

Uses a glasses-wearing thought experiment to make a technical comparison-group problem intuitive: once almost everyone wears glasses, the remaining non-wearers are no longer a meaningful baseline for judging glasses' effect.

Explicitly separates 'performing better than the remaining non-users' from 'performing better than the average student would perform without technology,' arguing PISA's methodology increasingly conflates the two as ed-tech becomes ubiquitous.
quotes: Across previous comparable PISA cycles, the relationship between classroom technology use and academic performance has been remarkably consistent: as technology use increases, performance largely declines.
These weren't three random countries: they were three of the four most technologically saturated education systems in the entire dataset.
In Japan, zero-use students still represented about 46% of test takers while in Denmark that value was only 0.6%. In other words, 'no technology use' no longer meant the same thing everywhere.

We test them again, and suddenly the glasses-wearing kids perform better. It would be tempting to conclude, 'Aha - glasses improve reading!' But there's a problem: who are the remaining 15% of students who aren't wearing glasses?

'Performing better than the remaining non-users' is not the same thing as 'performing better than the average student would perform without technology.' Unfortunately, we are rapidly losing the data needed to distinguish between the two.
